passages.original: Hæc autem sunt, quod in Tusculano ad suum studium uterque libros evolverit. Quodque Trebatius casu in Aristotelis Topica inciderit, et quod titulum operis admiratus, a M.Tullio inscriptionis sententiam perquisierit.Illud etiam quod ei Cicero se exposuisse commemorat,inveniendorum argumentorum illis libris scientiam contineri,ut sine ullo errore ad argumentorum inventionem via quadam et recto filo atque artificio veniretur,quae res breviter enuntiata,velut intentio- nem operis monstrat,eL docilem perficit auditorem. In hoc namque videtur esse comprehensum quae sit intenLio Topicorum,quoniam Cicero ait disciplinam esse in veniendorum argumentorum,non ut inveniantur(id enim natura suppeditat).Sed ut sine ullo labore,ac sine ulla confusione non casu ad ea mens, sed quadam via et ratione perveniat,post hanc benevolentiæ captationem,Trebatiilaudem subjungit, cum ejus verecundiam in his commemoratexpetendis, quae si postulanti amico Cicero praestitisset et gloriae praemium ferret et gratiae, sed quod petenti Trebatio, ut ei Topica traderet minime concessit.Id non proprii laboris fuga, sed Trebatii potius causa factum esse contendit,ut in eo quoque Trebatii velutituncrepulsi subiratus forsitananimus,nuncnon sit alienus.
passages.english: These are the facts: that at Tusculum each of them was unrolling books for his own study; that Trebatius happened to come upon Aristotle's Topics; and that, puzzled by the title of the work, he asked Marcus Tullius what the inscription meant. There is also the point that Cicero recalls he explained to him that those books contained the science of finding arguments, so that one might arrive at the discovery of arguments without any error, by a kind of path, a straight thread and a method. This, stated briefly, shows as it were the aim of the work and makes the listener receptive. For in this seems to be contained what the aim of the Topics is, since Cicero says that it is a discipline of finding arguments, not so that they may be found (for nature supplies that), but so that the mind may arrive at them without any labour and without any confusion, not by chance but by a certain path and method. After this winning of goodwill he adds praise of Trebatius, recalling his modesty in asking for these things. Had Cicero granted them to his friend's request, he would have gained the reward both of glory and of gratitude; but as to the fact that he did not at all comply when Trebatius asked him to teach him the Topics, he maintains that this was done not to avoid labour of his own, but rather for Trebatius' sake, so that in this too Trebatius' mind, which perhaps was somewhat angered at being, as it were, rebuffed at the time, might now not be estranged.
passages.notes: Scanning errors silently corrected (e.g. 'intentionem', 'et docilem', 'commemorat expetendis', 'veluti tunc repulsi subiratus forsitan animus, nunc'). 'in veniendorum' read as 'inveniendorum'.

passages.original: Ut enim dictum est, a Peripateticis haec ratio diligens disserendilogice vocatur, continens in se inveniendi judicandique peritiam.Stoici vero hanc eamdem rationem disserendi paulo angustius tractavero, nihil enim de inventione laborantes, in sola tantum judicatione consistunt,deque ea praecepta multipliciterdantes,dialecticam nuncupaverunt.Platoetiam dialecticam vocat facultatem quae id quod unum est possit in plura partiri,veluti soletgenus perproprias differentias usque ad ultimas speciesseparari,atque ea quae multa sunt, in unum generum ratione colligere.Hanc igitur Plato dialecticam dicit; Aristoteles vero logicam vocat, quam (ut dictum est) Cicero definivit diligentem disserendi rationem. Et hujus uno quidem modo trina partitio est: omnis namque vis logicae disciplinae aut definit aliquid, aut partitur, aut colligit. Colligendi autem facultas triplici diversit ate tractatur: aut enim veris ac necessariis argumentationibus disputatio decurrit,et disciplina vel demonstrationuncupatur;
passages.english: For, as has been said, by the Peripatetics this careful method of discourse is called logic, containing within it the skill of finding and of judging. The Stoics, however, treated this same method of discourse somewhat more narrowly: taking no trouble over discovery, they rest solely on judgement, and, giving many precepts about it, they named it dialectic. Plato too calls dialectic the faculty that can divide what is one into many, as a genus is usually separated through its proper differentiae down to the lowest species, and can gather what are many into one by the principle of genera. This, then, Plato calls dialectic; Aristotle calls it logic, which (as has been said) Cicero defined as the careful method of discourse. And of this there is, in one way, a threefold division: for the whole power of the logical discipline either defines something, or divides, or infers. The faculty of inferring is treated in three different ways: either the disputation proceeds by true and necessary argumentations, and it is called discipline or demonstration;
passages.notes: 'tractavero' read as 'tractavere' (treated).

passages.original: Ut igitur earum rerum quæ ahsconditæ sunt demonstrato et notato loco facilis inventio est, sic cum pervestigare argumentumaliquodvolumus, locos nosse debemus. Sic enim appellat sunt ab Aristotele hæ quasi sedes, e guibus argumenta promuntur, Itaque licet definirelocumesse argumenti sedemjargumentum autem rationem ,quæ rei dubix faciat fidem.
passages.english: Therefore, just as the discovery of things that are hidden is easy once their place has been shown and marked, so when we wish to track down some argument, we ought to know the places (loci). For this is what Aristotle called these, as it were, seats from which arguments are drawn. Thus one may define a place (locus) as the seat of an argument, and an argument as a reasoning that produces belief about a doubtful matter.
passages.notes: 'appellatae sunt' read for 'appellat sunt'. Locus renders Greek topos ('topic').

passages.original: Post diffinitionem loci atque argumenti facitplenissimam divisionem locorurn.Acprimum quoniam omnis divisio cuncta debet amplecti, neque superfluum quidquam interponere, nec omittere quid sit necessarium,id M. Tullius proposita divisione patefacit dicens : Ex his locis in quibus argumenta inclusa sunt, alios in eo ipso de quo agitur haerere, alios extrinsecus assumi.Nihil enim huic divisioni posse videtur addi vel minui,quandoquidembreviter cuncta complectitur. Argumentorum enim loci quicunque sumuntur, aui in ipso de quo agiturhcerent, aut minime.
passages.english: After the definition of place and argument he makes a most complete division of the places. And first, since every division ought to embrace everything, and neither insert anything superfluous nor omit anything necessary, Marcus Tullius makes this plain by setting out the division, saying: of these places in which arguments are contained, some inhere in the very thing under discussion, others are taken from outside. For nothing seems capable of being added to or taken from this division, since it briefly embraces everything. For whatever places of arguments are taken, they either inhere in the very thing under discussion, or they do not.

passages.original: Non enim sibi ipse testimonia parat orator,sed paratis utitur,nec ipse judicium facit,sed jam posito ac spontaneo rumore veniente utitur ad causam. Atque idcirco hos locos Græci ἀτέχνους vocant, id est inartificiales,atque,ut Tullius dixit,artis expertes. Quae enim non proprio oratoris artificio comparantur,sedseextrinsecusvenientiasubministrant, hæc jure artisexpertia sunt appellata. Hujus exemplum est:
passages.english: For the orator does not prepare testimonies for himself, but uses those already prepared; nor does he himself create a judgement, but uses for his case a rumour already established and arising of its own accord. And for this reason the Greeks call these places atechnoi, that is, 'inartificial', and, as Tullius said, 'without art'. For things that are not procured by the orator's own skill, but supply themselves coming from outside, are rightly called without art. An example of this is:
passages.notes: The passage breaks off before the example.

passages.original: Omne elementum priacipium est ejus rei cujus elementum esse perpenditur.Namejus quod ex elementis fit,ipsa elementa necesse est loco esse principii ; ergo quoniam hi loci superius designati argumentorum quasi quaedam principia'sunt (ipsi enim sunt qui continentargumenta; omne autem quod continet,ejus quod continetur principium est), idcirco ait Cicero veluti quædam elementa argumentorum videri locos hos quos superius posuit. Cautis- simeque adjecit, quasi qu ædam elementa ; non enim integre elementa,sed quasi in similitudine elementorum sunt hi loci qui in argumentis efficiendis sumuntur.
passages.english: Every element is a principle of that thing of which it is judged to be the element. For of what is made from elements, the elements themselves must stand in the position of a principle. Therefore, since these places designated above are, as it were, certain principles of arguments (for it is they that contain arguments, and everything that contains is a principle of what is contained), for that reason Cicero says that these places which he set out above seem to be, as it were, certain elements of arguments. And he very cautiously added 'as it were certain elements'; for these places that are taken in producing arguments are not wholly elements, but are so after a likeness to elements.

passages.original: Ex tot enim definitionum partibus argumenta producet, quantas quis definitionum partes esse cognoverit. Is vero habebit plurimam talium locorum facultalem, quem definitionum diversitas non latebit. Ob hoc igitur M. Tullius,quos confuse atque indigeste posuit locos,nunc eosdem diligentiore ratione partitur.Ac primum illud propensiore consideratione tractandum est,quod,ut dictum est, etiam loci ipsi res quaedam sunt,sed tunc esse intelliguntur loci,cum ab his trahitur argumentum.
passages.english: For a person will produce arguments from as many parts of definitions as he has come to know there are parts of definitions. And he will have the greatest supply of such places from whom the diversity of definitions is not hidden. For this reason, then, Marcus Tullius now divides by a more careful method the same places which he set out in a confused and disordered way. And first this must be treated with closer consideration: that, as has been said, the places themselves are also certain things, but they are understood to be places when an argument is drawn from them.

passages.original: Tullium ad hominum protulisse opinionem,non ad veritatem. Nam ut inter optime philosophantes constilit,illa maxime sunt quæ longe a sensibus segregata sunt, illa minus, quae opiniones sensibus subministrant. Unde etiam idem Cicero in Timceo Platonis ait: Quid est quod semper sit, nec ullum habeat ortum, et quod gignatur, nec unquam sit? Quorum alterum,intelligentiae ratione comprehenditur,alterum afFert opinionem sensui rationis expers. HicigiLur id quod semper sit,rationi adjecit, id vero quod nunquam sit,sensibus conjunxit.
passages.english: [It should be known that M.] Tullius spoke according to people's opinion, not according to the truth. For as is agreed among the best philosophers, those things most truly are which are far removed from the senses, and those less so which supply opinions to the senses. Hence the same Cicero also says in [his translation of] Plato's Timaeus: 'What is it that always is and has no origin, and what is it that comes to be and never is? Of these the one is grasped by the reasoning of the intellect, the other brings about opinion in sense, which lacks reason.' Here, then, he assigned what always is to reason, and joined what never is to the senses.
passages.notes: Opening 'M.' belongs to the preceding sentence in context.

passages.original: Ut igitur minuatur animal et homini coæquetur, addimus differentiam, qua adjuncta,rerum quidem numerus crescit,vis autem rei atque amplitudo minuitur.Addo igitur rationale, efficioque animal rationale.Minus est igitur animal rationale quam proprie animal. Dico autem homi- nem esse animal rationale.Sed id nondum coaequatur ad hominem,possunt enim esse animalia rationabilia, sicut Platoni quoque de astris placet, quae homines non sunt. Addo igitur rursus aliam dilferentiam,si quoquo modo iterum definitio contrahatur,ut fiat homini quod definitur aequale ; adjungo igitur mortale,ac dico hominem esse animal rationate mortale,id aequatur ad hominem.
passages.english: So, to reduce 'animal' and make it equal to man, we add a differentia; when it is added, the number of terms grows, but the scope and extent of the thing diminishes. I add, then, 'rational', and produce 'rational animal'. 'Rational animal' is therefore less than 'animal' strictly. Now I say that man is a rational animal. But this is not yet made equal to man, for there can be rational animals which are not men, as Plato too holds about the stars. So I add again another differentia, so that the definition may be contracted once more in some way, and what is defined may become equal to man: I add 'mortal' and say that man is a rational mortal animal; this is equal to man.

passages.original: Dico igitur hominis hanc esse definitionem quae ex pluribus communibus junctis unum tamen quiddam homini proprium atque aequale conficit.Atque in cæteris definitionibus eadem ratio est, ut definitiones fiant collectiscommunitatibus, in unumquecopue copatis, cum necesse sit illa copulatione quae communia sunt conlrabi atque in minorem cohiberi modum, eiquc quod definitur ex communitatibus junctis aliquid proprium atque æquale conponitur. Hoc est igitur quod ait Cicero,hunc esse definitionis modum,cum sumpseris ea quae sint ei rei quam defiinre velis cum aliis communia, usque eo persequi, ut propriurr. efficiatur,quod in nullam aliam rem trans. ferri possit, ut his verbis et hac sententia breviter significare videatur hanc esse definitionem q uæ,ex substantialibus communitatibus juncta atque in minorem modum redacta,fitei rei quæ definitur a qualis.Exempla vero quae ponit hujusmodi sunt,unum definiendae hæreditatis, alterum gentilitatis : Haere- ditatis quidem hoc modo : Hæreditas est pecunia.
passages.english: I say, then, that this is the definition of man, which from several common [terms] joined together nevertheless produces one thing proper to man and equal to him. And in other definitions the method is the same: definitions are made by gathering common [features] and coupling them into one, since by that coupling the common features must be contracted and confined to a narrower measure, and from the joined common features something proper and equal is composed for what is defined. This, then, is what Cicero says, that this is the method of definition: when you have taken those things which the thing you wish to define has in common with others, to pursue them until something proper results which cannot be transferred to any other thing; so that by these words and this thought he seems briefly to indicate that a definition is that which, joined from substantial common features and reduced to a narrower measure, becomes equal to the thing defined. The examples he gives are of this kind, one of defining inheritance, the other of clanship (gentilitas). Of inheritance thus: Inheritance is property.
passages.notes: 'in unumque copulatis' read for 'in unumquecopue copatis'. Pecunia here means property/estate, not only money.

passages.original: Interpretatio vero nominis ἐτυμολογία Grcece.Latine veriloquium nuncupatur; έ̔τυμον enim verum significat, λóγος orationem.Sed quia id veriloquium minus in uso Latini sermonis habebatur, interpretatione nominis notationem Tullius appellat. Ea est hujusmodi, ut si quaeras quid est postliminium. In qua quæstione non illud videtur inquiri quae res postliminio revertantur, hoc enim in divisionem caderet,id estearum omnium rerum enumerationem quae postliminio redeunt poslulareLVelut si ita dicamus : Postliminio redeunt homo, navis, mulus clitellarius, equus,equa quæ frenos recipere solet, id est domita, nunc enumeratæ sunt res quæ postliminio revertantur.
passages.english: The interpretation of a name is called in Greek *etymologia*, in Latin *veriloquium* ["true-speaking"]; for *etymon* means "true" and *logos* "speech". But because this word *veriloquium* was little used in the Latin language, Tullius calls the interpretation of a name *notatio*. It is of this kind: as if you were to ask what *postliminium* is. In this question what seems to be investigated is not which things return by *postliminium*, for that would fall under division, that is, it would demand an enumeration of all the things that return by *postliminium*. For instance, if we were to say: "By *postliminium* there return a man, a ship, a pack-mule, a horse, a mare that is accustomed to take the bridle, that is, a broken one," then the things that return by *postliminium* have been enumerated.
passages.notes: *Postliminium*: the Roman legal right by which a person or property captured by the enemy recovered former status on return. Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'Grcece' for 'Graece', 'poslulareL' for 'postulare').

passages.original: sive partium conjunctione completur, ut totum.At verohreo divisio generis incujuspartes quælibet illa res de quacontenditurincludenda est,non id efficit, ut totius substantia constituatur, sed ut illud quod approbare quaerimus intra genus collocetur. Quem argumentationis modum imprimis M. Tullius vaHdum esse confirmat. Illa enim regula salis vera est atque necessaria. Quae de genere prædicantur, eadem de specie modis omnibus prsedicari. Illud vero quaeri perutile est, cum aliquid de particularibus rebus probatur ex superposita proxima specie, ut si Socratem rationalem esse approbemus, quoniam sit homo, cum sit homo rationalis, ulrum ex genere an ex forma argumentum ductum esse arbitremur. Nam sidicamusexgenere, ultima species genus esse non potest; si exspecie,superpositum genus semper species probare desiderat.
passages.english: or [whether it be a whole that] is completed by the conjunction of parts, as a whole [is]. But the division of a genus, in any one of whose parts the thing under dispute is to be included, does not bring it about that the substance of a whole is constituted, but that what we seek to prove is placed within the genus. This mode of argumentation Marcus Tullius confirms to be valid above all. For that rule is quite true and necessary: what is predicated of the genus is in every way predicated also of the species. But it is very useful to ask, when something is proved about particular things from the proximate species placed above [them], as if we prove that Socrates is rational because he is a man, since man is rational, whether we should judge the argument to be drawn from the genus or from the form. For if we say [it is drawn] from the genus, the last species cannot be a genus; if from the species, a species always seeks to prove the genus placed above it.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'verohreo' read as 'vero haec/hic', 'vaHdum' as 'validum', 'salis' as 'satis', 'ulrum' as 'utrum'). The last clause ('superpositum genus semper species probare desiderat') is obscure and possibly corrupt; the sense seems to be that an argument 'from the species' would normally have a species proving something about a genus placed above it, or that what is placed above should be a genus. Translated literally.

passages.original: Nam cum in pluribus rebus (ides praestari debeat, unaquesimilitudo sit in fide praestanda tam in tutore quam socio, atque eo cui mandatum sit, eoque quifiduciam acceperit,debet eadem similitudo procuratori etiam convenire.Fiduciamvero accepit cuicunque res aliqua mancipatur, ut eam mancipanti remancipct, velut si quis tempus dubium ti- mens amico potentiori fundum mancipet, utei cum tempus quod suspectum esL præterierit reddat; haec mancipatio fiduciaria nominatur, idcirco quod restituendi fides interponitur. Hæc similitudinis collectione plurimum Socrates esse usus dicitur, ut in Platonis aliorumque ejus sectatorum voluminibus invenitur.Quoties vero una res uni rei per simililudinem comparatur, hoc modo colligitur argumentum. Regendorum finium arbitri esse dicuntur,quifinalia litigia discernunt, ut si fuerit de finibus orta contentio, eorum dirtmaturarbitrio.Sed fines in agrorum tantum limitibusesse dicuntur,arbitri autemfmiun] regendorum in civitate esse non possunt.
passages.english: For since in many relationships good faith ought to be maintained, and there is one likeness in maintaining good faith, as much in a guardian as in a partner, and in one to whom a commission has been given, and in one who has received [property] in trust, the same likeness ought also to apply to an agent. Now a person has received [property] in trust whenever some thing is conveyed to him by *mancipatio* on condition that he convey it back to the one who conveyed it; for instance, if someone, fearing an uncertain time, conveys an estate to a more powerful friend, so that he may return it to him when the time that is feared has passed. This conveyance is called fiduciary, because a pledge of restitution is interposed. Socrates is said to have made very great use of this gathering of likenesses, as is found in the books of Plato and of his other followers. But whenever one thing is compared with one other thing by likeness, the argument is gathered in this way. Those who decide boundary disputes are called arbiters for regulating boundaries, so that if a contention has arisen about boundaries, it is settled by their decision. But boundaries are said to exist only in the limits of fields, and arbiters for regulating boundaries cannot exist in a city.
passages.notes: '(ides' read as 'fides'; 'fmiun]' as 'finium'; 'dirtmatur' as 'dirimatur'. *Mancipatio*: formal Roman conveyance of property.

passages.original: Tullius re quidem Aristoteli fere consentit, sed ab eo nominum interpretatione diversus est.Nam quae Aristoteles opposita, id est ὰντιϰείμ£va, vocat, ea Tullius contraria nominat; sed haec paulo posterius. Nunc Aristotelis divisio consideretur.Oppositorum igitur secundum Aristotelem alia sunt contraria, alia privatio et habitus, alia relativa,alia contradictoria. Contraria quidem, ut album atque nigrum ; habitus vcro et privatio, ut visus et caecitas, dignitas et indignitas ;
passages.english: [...] Tullius agrees with Aristotle almost entirely in substance, but differs from him in the interpretation of terms. For what Aristotle calls opposites, that is *antikeimena*, Tullius names contraries; but of this a little later. Now let Aristotle's division be considered. Of opposites, then, according to Aristotle, some are contraries, some privation and possession, some relatives, some contradictories. Contraries, as white and black; possession and privation, as sight and blindness, worthiness and unworthiness;
passages.notes: The sentence begins in the preceding context ('quanquam M.'), i.e. 'although Marcus Tullius...'.

passages.original: Si stullitiam fugimus, sapientiam sequamur; si bonitatem appetimus, malitiam fugiamus, quanquam malitia quoque,secundum eumdem modum qui superius dictus est, privationibus possit adjungi.Privantia vero secundum Ciceronem sunt, quae Græce στερητιϰά appellantur, quæhabent eam partem orationis præpositam, quæ cum fuerit adjecta, semper fere aliquid demit ut ea(in) praepositiojhcec enim syllaba cui fuerit apposita,demit fere aliquid ex ea vi quam esset res quælibet habitura, si in syllabam præpositam non haberet,ut humanitati inhumanitas : in namque praeposita id de quo dicitur humanitate privavit, ut dignitas, indignitas;et Tullius quidem ea tantum privantia esse confirmat, in quibuscunque syllaba ista praeponilur : privantium quippe naturasecundumTullium hujus syllabae commemoratione finitur ;
passages.english: If we flee folly, let us pursue wisdom; if we seek goodness, let us flee wickedness, although wickedness too, in the same way as was said above, could be joined to privations. Privatives, according to Cicero, are those called in Greek *sterētika*, which have prefixed that part of speech which, when added, almost always takes something away, such as the preposition *in*: for this syllable, to whatever it is attached, takes away to some extent from the force that the thing would have had if it did not have the syllable *in* prefixed, as *inhumanitas* [inhumanity] to *humanitas* [humanity]: for *in*, prefixed, has deprived what it is said of of humanity; likewise *dignitas*, *indignitas* [worthiness, unworthiness]. And Tullius affirms that only those are privatives in which this syllable is prefixed; for according to Tullius the nature of privatives is defined by mention of this syllable;

passages.original: est,juris enim peritus de facti qualitatc, non etiam de ipsius facti veritate respondet. Idcirco quoties ad Gallum peritum juris facti quaestiodeferebatur,nihil ad nos inquiebat,etad Ciceronem potius consulcntes, id est ad rhetorem remittebat. In quo Tullius facere ad Trebatium locum miscuit dicens. Quanquam locus hic ab adjunctis conjecturalibus causis maxime utilis, nihil consultorum juris prudentiam juvet, patiere me tamen, inquit, nullam suscepti operis partem præterire, ne si in hoc Iibro nihil praeter ture artis exempla conscripsero, tuae tantum gratiae videatur addictus, ab adjunctis vero locus qui non modo jurisconsultis, sed ne philosophis quidem praeter oratores non patet, trium saepe temporum ratione tractandus est.
passages.english: [...] for the legal expert gives an opinion on the quality of a deed, not also on the truth of the deed itself. Therefore whenever a question of fact was brought to Gallus, the legal expert, he used to say, "This has nothing to do with us," and would send those consulting him to Cicero instead, that is, to the orator. On this point Tullius has inserted a passage directed at Trebatius, saying: "Although this topic from adjuncts, very useful in conjectural cases, is of no help to the jurisprudence of legal consultants, you will nevertheless allow me," he says, "to pass over no part of the work I have undertaken, lest, if I write nothing in this book except examples from your art, it should seem devoted only to your favour. The topic from adjuncts, then, which is open not only not to jurisconsults but not even to philosophers, except to orators, must often be treated with reference to the three times."
passages.notes: The opening 'est' completes a sentence begun in the preceding context. The quoted words paraphrase Cicero, Topica; 'ture' read as 'tuae'.

passages.original: positionis superius constitutæ, dicamque, sed diesj est, ac tunc demum id quod est in quæstione con- : cludam, lux est igitur,Ergo cum ad syllogismi conclusionem,et tota enuntiatione in proponendo, et in assumendo parte enuntiationis utamur, necesse est ut eaquibus utimur nil habeant dubitabile,siquidem ex his ea quae suntambigua capientfidem.Quod si propositio aliquoties quidem per se nota est atque perspicua, aliquoties vero probationis indigens invenitur,assumptioquuqu.e aliquoties per se vera esse notabituraliquotiesapprobationis indigetadjumentis. Quo fit ut si et propositio et assumptio demonstrandae sint, quinquepartitus (ut Cicero etiam in Rhetoricis auctor est) syllogismus fiat, constans ex propositione ejusque probaLione,assumptione,ejusdemque probatione, et conclusione. Quod si neutra sit approbanda,tripartitus sit, ex propositione scilicet, assumptione et conclusione.
passages.english: [...] of the proposition set out above, and I shall say, "But it is day," and only then conclude what is in question: "Therefore there is light." Since, then, for the conclusion of a syllogism we use the whole statement in the proposition and part of the statement in the assumption, it is necessary that the things we use contain nothing doubtful, since from them the things that are ambiguous will gain credence. But if the proposition is sometimes known and evident by itself, but sometimes is found to need proof, the assumption too will sometimes be recognised as true by itself and sometimes need the aids of proof. Hence if both proposition and assumption must be demonstrated, the syllogism becomes fivefold (as Cicero also states in the Rhetorica), consisting of the proposition and its proof, the assumption and its proof, and the conclusion. But if neither needs to be proved, it is threefold, namely of proposition, assumption and conclusion.
passages.notes: Opening words continue a sentence from the preceding context ('I shall assume one part...').

passages.original: Tullii verbis mediocris lucem commentationis interseram.Septem igitur modoshypotheticos enumerans ait, cum in connexis propositionibus id quod est primum assumitur, ut ostendatur secundum, primum a dialecticis modum vocari, hoc modo : Si hoc est,illud est; quod dicit hoc,primum est,quod vero ait ilJud,secundum.Assumatur ergo quod primum est,alqui hoc est; concluditur igitur id quod secundum est, illud igitur est, velut in his rursus exemplis : si homo est,animal est,assumitur,atqui homo est,concluditur,animal igitur est. Secundum vero modum ait esse Tullius connexis propositionibus textum, in quo si secundum negatur, sequitur ut id etiam quod primum est abnuatur hoc modo; si hoc est,iilud est: illud autem non est,igiturnehoc quidem est. In exemplis ita : si homo est;
passages.english: [...] I shall insert into the words of Tullius the light of a modest commentary. Enumerating, then, seven hypothetical modes, he says that when, in conditional propositions, what is first is assumed in order to show the second, this is called by the dialecticians the first mode, in this way: "If this is, that is"; where he says "this" is the first, where he says "that" is the second. Let what is first be assumed, then: "But this is"; what is second is concluded: "Therefore that is"; as again in these examples: "If it is a man, it is an animal"; it is assumed: "But it is a man"; it is concluded: "Therefore it is an animal." The second mode, Tullius says, is woven of conditional propositions, in which, if the second is denied, it follows that what is first is also rejected, in this way: "If this is, that is; but that is not; therefore this is not either." In examples, thus: "If it is a man,
passages.notes: The opening sentence begins in the preceding context ('M.' = Marcus).

passages.original: Sed haec an sola beatos efficere possit, quaeritur an ei sintextrinsecusaddenda quae juvent, vel fortunae bona, vel corporis, itaque ea causa quae vi sua efficit aliquid, aut talis est, ut ei nulla sint extrinsecus adjumenta quaerenda, veluti artifici instrumenta quaedam, qui- , bus id quod efficiendum est explicet atque conformet.Earum vero omnium quae Tullius statuit in alterutra divisione causarum,illa quidem quæ vi sua explicant ea quorum causas sunt,omnia tam per se ad efficiendum valentia, quam quaesiti extrinsecus juvaminis indigentia, in ea Aristotelicae divisionis causa locabuntur,quæ est principium motus.Quanquam de sapientia tali causae nou convenit exemplum,sed potius ad rationem formamquecontendit. Namque sapientia ratione quadam atque forma efficit sapientes.Ejus vero causae quam Tullius refert, sine qua non fit aliquid,materia quidem, tempus et locus,id est, ex quo fit, vel in quo fit, quae sunt efficienti substantia naturæ : ut uno intellectu com- prehendantur,vel materia sunt,velmatenaevicesupposita;
passages.english: But whether this [wisdom] alone can make people happy, it is asked whether things should be added to it from outside to help it, either goods of fortune or of the body. And so the cause which produces something by its own force is either such that no external aids need be sought for it, or [such as needs them], like certain tools for a craftsman, with which he works out and shapes what is to be made. Of all the causes which Tullius sets out in either division of causes, those which by their own force bring about the things of which they are causes, both those capable of producing by themselves and those needing help sought from outside, will be placed in that cause of Aristotle's division which is the principle of motion. Although the example of wisdom does not fit such a cause, but rather tends towards the formal reason; for wisdom makes people wise by a certain reason and form. Of the cause which Tullius mentions, without which something does not come about, matter, time and place, that is, that out of which something comes and that in which it comes, which are substance to the efficient nature: so that they may be grasped in one notion, they are either matter or put in place of matter;
passages.notes: The sentence 'itaque ea causa ... aut talis est' seems to lack its second alternative; I supply it in brackets. The last sentence is syntactically loose; 'efficienti substantia naturae' is uncertain.

passages.original: Haec enim ut aliquid efficiatur, movendi principium sunt, at in arte, vel habitu, vel natura, illa causa est, quae in ratione consistit. Species enim ac ratio uniuscujusque efficiendae rei in arte et habituet natura posita est. Casus vero exterior causa, nec inter principales annumeratur secundum Aristotelem .Secund um vero M. Tullium casus est latens effectae rei causa ;quod quale sit paulo postorius designabitur.
passages.english: For these are the principle of motion, so that something may be brought about; but in art, or disposition, or nature, that cause is the one which consists in a rational principle. For the form and rational principle of each thing to be made lies in art, disposition and nature. Chance, however, is an external cause, and is not counted among the principal ones according to Aristotle. But according to Marcus Tullius chance is the hidden cause of a thing brought about; what kind of thing this is will be shown a little later.
passages.notes: 'Haec' refers to causes from will or emotion in the preceding context. 'posterius' read for 'postorius'.

passages.original: Bene autem ac facile nemo efficit, nisi artis ratione fuerit instructus.Cum igitur totius operis haec sit intentio, ut argumenta quae confusa etveluti clausa natura suppeditat, artificialiter vestigentur, quid sit per quod efficere id quod promittit ars valeat,sub exempli notatione demonstrat : ut enim facilius argumenta reperiantur,illa res efficiet, si demonstrentur lociin quibus argumenta sunt collocata.Etenim ut si quis aliquid quærat, facilius id investigare possit atque invenire, si locus ei monstretur ubi sit positum id quod inquirit; ita etiam cum quis argumentum invenire conatur, si ei locus ubi argumentum sit positum, declaretur,f'aciliusargumentum quod quærit valebit invenire. Ita enim Aristoteles, et ita Tullius appellat eas sedes in quibus argumenta suntcollocata, id est locos, qui ab Aristotele topica vocati sunt. Sed quoniam de sedibusargumentorumloquimurshicujusmodisintpaulo altius expediamus ; locus enim non uno modo intelligitur.
passages.english: But no one produces [anything] well and easily unless he has been equipped with the method of an art. Since, then, the aim of the whole work is that arguments which nature supplies in confused and as it were locked-up form should be tracked down by art, he shows by means of an example what it is through which the art can achieve what it promises: for what will make arguments easier to find is that the places in which arguments are located be shown. For just as, if someone is looking for something, he can track it down and find it more easily if the place where what he seeks is put is shown to him, so also when someone tries to find an argument, if the place where the argument is put is made clear to him, he will be able more easily to find the argument he seeks. For so Aristotle, and so Tullius, names those seats in which arguments are located, that is, places (*loci*), which were called *topica* by Aristotle. But since we are speaking of the seats of arguments, let us explain a little more deeply of what kind they are; for 'place' is not understood in only one way.

passages.original: Diviso causarum loco atque ordine suis partibus distributo,de loci ejusdem facultate, quibusque uberius,quibusque angustius accommodetur, uti saepe Ciceroni mos est, disserit. Primum enim, inquit, oratoribus ac philosophis, quorum in disputationibus larga materia est,multa ex causaru m loco argumentorum sup petit copia. Communis quippe oratoribus ac philosophis bic locus esse prospicitur qui est a eausis,his naturas rerum quod est philosophiae proprium.
passages.english: Having divided the topic of causes and arranged its order into its parts, he discusses, as is often Cicero's custom, the power of this same topic, and to which matters it is applied more fully and to which more narrowly. For first, he says, orators and philosophers, whose disputations have ample material, are supplied with a great abundance of arguments from the topic of causes. Indeed this topic, which is drawn from causes, is seen to be common to orators and philosophers: to the latter when they [prove] the natures of things, which is proper to philosophy,
passages.notes: The sentence continues into the following context ('to the former, which belongs to oratorical skill, when they prove deeds'); 'prove' is supplied from there. Scanning errors corrected (bic = hic, eausis = causis).

passages.original: Necessariarum pars in vi, pars in scientia posita est.Effecta vero intantum dividi possunt,inquantum ad superius dictas causas referuntur. Locus vero a comparatione minorum, parium atque majorum,dividitur in numerum ,speciem,vim, ad res alias affectionem.Quæ cum ita sint. cumque nihil sit in divisione prætermissum,recte M. Tullius partitionem eonclusit,dicens nullam argumenti sedem esse præteritam.Reotat igitur locus qui extrinsecus sumitur, quem, quoniam nihil jurisconsultis est utilis, non Trebatii causa, sed ne quid perfecto operi deesse videatur, adjungit.
passages.english: Of the necessary [causes], some lie in force, some in knowledge. Effects, however, can be divided to the extent that they are referred to the causes mentioned above. The topic from the comparison of lesser, equal and greater things is divided into number, kind, force, and relation to other things. Since this is so, and since nothing has been passed over in the division, Marcus Tullius rightly concluded the partition, saying that no seat of argument had been omitted. There remains, then, the topic that is taken from outside, which, since it is of no use to jurists, he adds not for Trebatius' sake, but so that nothing may seem to be lacking from a complete work.
passages.notes: 'Reotat' read as 'Restat'; 'eonclusit' as 'conclusit'.

passages.original: Neque enim hunc esse Trebatium, qui sua arte contentus, caeterorum studia negligat, verum diligentia atque inge- nio plurimum valens,cuncta ase pertinere ducat, quae liberalibus studiis annumerentur : simul dandam esse operam dicit,quoniarn benevolo animo Ciceronis opus Trebatius esset editurus, ut cum in multorum manus venisset,prodesse iis integrum posset, qui rectis studiis tenerentur, hoc quoque Trebatio beneficii nomine concedens,quod ad eum scripta,et per eum edita plurimis profutura conscriberet.
passages.english: For [he says that] Trebatius is not the sort of man who, content with his own art, neglects the studies of others, but one who, being very strong in diligence and talent, considers everything counted among the liberal studies to concern himself. At the same time he says that effort must be taken, since Trebatius was going to publish Cicero's work with a kindly mind, so that when it came into the hands of many it might be of benefit, complete, to those who were engaged in right studies; granting this also to Trebatius by way of a favour, that he was composing writings addressed to him and published through him which would be of use to very many.
passages.notes: 'ase' read as 'a se'; 'quoniarn' as 'quoniam'.

passages.original: Extrinsecus positum argumenti locum, quem M. Tullius vocat artis expertem, in testimonio positum ! esse pronuntiat. Dubitari autem potest quid hic locus a superioribus differat, quos in affectis locavit. Nam uti affecta semper in relatione sunt constituta, ita etiam testimonia ad ea quorum sunt testimonia referuntur.
passages.english: He declares that the topic of argument placed outside, which Marcus Tullius calls 'without art', consists in testimony. But it can be doubted how this topic differs from the earlier ones which he placed among the related things. For just as related things are always constituted in relation, so too testimonies are referred to the things of which they are testimonies.
passages.notes: 'affecta' rendered 'related things' (things in a state of relation). A stray '!' after 'positum' omitted.

passages.original: quæ autem necessitas extorquet,ipso quo- dammodovidetur veritas dicere,atque ideo eis veluti auctoritate subnixis fides adhibetur.Concursio etiam rerum fortuitarum facit fidem,quæ cum aliquoties falsa designet,tamen ita est vehemens,ut se ab ea veritas explicare vix possit.Quale est quod de Pal a- mede narratur.Pbryx exstinctus,qui quasi a Priamo missus videretur, repertae Priami litteræ Phrygia manus imitata,quæ concurrentia fidem facerent proditionis.Hinc dicit Cicero : Talis etiam fortuitarum rerum concursio est ".
passages.english: but what necessity wrings out, the truth itself seems in a way to speak, and therefore belief is given to such things as if supported by authority. A concurrence of chance events also produces belief; although it sometimes indicates falsehoods, it is nonetheless so forceful that truth can scarcely extricate itself from it. Such is what is told of Palamedes: a Phrygian killed, who would seem to have been sent as it were by Priam; a letter of Priam found, written in an imitation of a Phrygian hand; things which, concurring, produced belief in treason. Hence Cicero says: 'Such too is the concurrence of chance events.'

passages.original: Opinio autem est,non modo eos virtutem habere quiha- beant ,sed eos etiam qui habere videantur.Itaque quos ingenio,quos studio, quos doctrina præditos vident, quo- rumque viam constantem e( probatum,ut Catonis,Læ- Iii, Scipiollis aliorumque plurium, videntur eis esse quales se ipsi velint. Nec solumeus censenllalesesse qui in honoribus populi reque publica versantur,sedet oratores, et philosophos, et poetas, et historicos, ex quorum et dictis et scriptis sxpe auctoritas petitur ad faciendam fidem.
passages.english: Now the opinion [of virtue] is held not only of those who have virtue, but also of those who seem to have it. And so those whom they see endowed with talent, with zeal, with learning, and whose life [they see] to be consistent and approved, like that of Cato, Laelius, Scipio and many others, seem to them to be such as they themselves would wish to be. And they consider to be such not only those who are engaged in the offices of the people and in public affairs, but also orators, philosophers, poets and historians, from whose sayings and writings authority is often sought to produce belief.
passages.notes: 'viam' read as 'vitam'. Badly scanned 'censenllalesesse' read as 'censent tales esse'.
